city_metadata.city_summary: New York, often called New York City (NYC), is the most populous city in the United States. It is located at the southern tip of New York State on New York Harbor, one of the world's largest natural harbors. The city comprises five boroughs, each coextensive with its respective county.

tags.name: Coney Island
tags.description: A retro beachfront amusement district with the historic Cyclone wooden roller coaster, the Wonder Wheel, a boardwalk, and Nathan's Famous original hot dog stand. It's a fun, slightly kitschy half-day trip from Manhattan by subway.

tags.name: The Vessel at Hudson Yards
tags.description: A honeycomb-like structure of interlocking staircases in the Hudson Yards development, offering unusual angles over the surrounding skyscrapers. Access has changed over the years due to safety concerns, so check current opening status before planning around it.

tags.name: Roosevelt Island Tramway
tags.description: An aerial cable car that glides over the East River between Manhattan and Roosevelt Island, giving unusual views of the Queensboro Bridge and Midtown skyline. It runs on the same fare as the subway, making it a cheap, quick way to see the city from above.

attractions.description: Summit One Vanderbilt is an interactive multi-sensory observation deck featuring fully mirrored rooms, transparent glass sky-boxes, and floating silver balloons.
The Staten Island Ferry is a passenger ferry line running 24/7 between Lower Manhattan and Staten Island, offering commuters and tourists completely free close-up views of the Statue of Liberty.

tags.name: Empire State Building
tags.description: The Art Deco skyscraper that defined the New York skyline since 1931, with observation decks on the 86th and 102nd floors. Sunset or early morning slots have the shortest lines and the best light for skyline photos.

attractions.description: Top of the Rock is an open-air observation deck atop Rockefeller Center, offering the city's most iconic view directly facing the Empire State Building and Central Park.
The Edge is the highest outdoor sky deck in the Western Hemisphere, suspended mid-air at 30 Hudson Yards with a thrilling glass-bottom floor looking straight down.

tags.name: Statue of Liberty & Ellis Island
tags.description: The iconic copper statue gifted by France in 1886, reachable only by ferry from Battery Park or Liberty State Park. Combine it with Ellis Island's immigration museum right next door — book tickets well in advance if you want to climb up to the crown or pedestal.

tags.name: 9/11 Memorial & Museum
tags.description: Twin reflecting pools mark the footprints of the original Twin Towers, surrounded by the names of everyone lost in the 2001 and 1993 attacks. The underground museum tells the story in detail through artifacts and recordings — plan for a couple of emotionally heavy hours.

tags.name: Brooklyn Bridge
tags.description: A 19th-century engineering marvel connecting Manhattan and Brooklyn, with a raised pedestrian walkway offering some of the city's best skyline views. Walk it around sunrise or sunset to avoid the daytime foot traffic, then reward yourself with pizza in DUMBO on the Brooklyn side.

tags.name: Times Square
tags.description: The neon-lit intersection often called 'The Crossroads of the World,' packed with billboards, Broadway theaters, and street performers around the clock. It's touristy and chaotic by design — go once for the spectacle, but don't expect an authentic New York meal here.

tags.name: Grand Central Terminal
tags.description: A beaux-arts train station famous for its main concourse ceiling painted with a constellation mural. Look for the Whispering Gallery near the Oyster Bar, where two people can hear each other whisper across a diagonal arch, and check out the food hall downstairs.

attractions.description: The Flatiron Building is a groundbreaking triangular wedge-shaped skyscraper completed in 1902, sitting prominently next to Madison Square Park as an architectural icon of Manhattan.
St. Patrick's Cathedral is a decorated Neo-Gothic Roman Catholic cathedral church on Fifth Avenue, serving as a prominent landmark nestled among Midtown's modern skyscrapers.
The Main Branch of the New York Public Library is a historic Beaux-Arts building guarded by the famous lion statues, featuring the cinematic and majestic Rose Main Reading Room.

tags.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
tags.description: One of the largest and most comprehensive art museums in the world, spanning 5,000 years of art from Egyptian antiquities to modern painting. It's genuinely too big to see in one visit, so it helps to pick two or three wings in advance rather than trying to see everything.

tags.name: Museum of Modern Art (MoMA)
tags.description: Home to some of the most recognizable works of modern art, including Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' and Warhol's soup cans. Buying timed tickets online in advance is worth it to skip the entry line, especially on weekends.

tags.name: American Museum of Natural History
tags.description: A massive museum famous for its dinosaur skeletons, the Hall of Ocean Life's giant blue whale model, and the Hayden Planetarium. It's a favorite for families, but the scale of the collection makes it worthwhile for adults too.

tags.name: Guggenheim Museum
tags.description: Frank Lloyd Wright's spiral-shaped building on Fifth Avenue is as much the attraction as the modern and contemporary art inside. The design lets you walk a continuous ramp down through the galleries rather than moving room to room.

tags.name: See a Broadway Show
tags.description: The Theater District around Times Square hosts dozens of long-running and new musicals and plays in historic venues. TKTS booths sell same-day discounted tickets if you're flexible on the show, otherwise book popular titles weeks or months ahead.

tags.name: The Cloisters
tags.description: A branch of the Met located in Fort Tryon Park at the northern tip of Manhattan, built from reassembled medieval European monasteries. It houses the famous Unicorn Tapestries and offers a quieter, more atmospheric museum experience than the main Met building.

attractions.description: The Intrepid Museum is a maritime history museum located on a historic WWII aircraft carrier, exhibiting an authentic space shuttle, a British Airways Concorde, and a submarine.
The Whitney Museum of American Art focuses on 20th and 21st-century American art, housed in an industrial-style building by Renzo Piano at the base of the High Line.
The Morgan Library & Museum is a majestic institution housing the private book collection of financier J. Pierpont Morgan, filled with rare illuminated manuscripts and historic triptychs.
The Brooklyn Museum is New York's second-largest art museum, holding vast holdings of ancient Egyptian antiquities and diverse global artistic traditions spanning centuries.
The Frick Collection is an internationally acclaimed museum housed in the gilded-age neoclassical mansion of industrialist Henry Clay Frick, displaying exquisite old master paintings.

tags.name: Central Park
tags.description: An 843-acre park in the middle of Manhattan with lakes, meadows, a zoo, and landmarks like Bethesda Terrace and Strawberry Fields. Renting a bike or rowboat, or just wandering the paths, is one of the best free things to do in the city.

tags.name: The High Line
tags.description: An elevated park built on a former freight rail line running through Chelsea, lined with gardens, public art, and views into the surrounding buildings. It connects nicely with Chelsea Market and the Whitney Museum at its southern end.

tags.name: Prospect Park
tags.description: Designed by the same architects as Central Park, this Brooklyn park feels wilder and less crowded, with a lake, woodland trails, and the Prospect Park Zoo. A good pick if you want a slower, more local feel than Manhattan's parks.

attractions.description: Bryant Park is a beloved French-style public park located in Midtown Manhattan, known for its lush green lawn, open-air summer movie screenings, and an iconic winter ice-skating rink.
The Battery is a historic waterfront park at the southern tip of Manhattan, offering harbor views, lush gardens, and serving as the departure hub for ferries to the Statue of Liberty.
Little Island is an innovative floating public park on the Hudson River, built on tulip-shaped architectural concrete pillars that create a dramatic landscape over the water.

tags.name: Governors Island
tags.description: A car-free island in New York Harbor, a short ferry ride from Manhattan, with historic forts, art installations, hammock groves, and skyline views. Rent a bike or just picnic on the lawns — it's especially pleasant in summer when it's open to visitors.

attractions.description: Washington Square Park is a dynamic public park in Greenwich Village, recognized by its historic marble memorial arch, lively fountain, street performers, and active chess players.
Brooklyn Botanic Garden is an urban botanical oasis containing specialty plant collections, a world-famous traditional Japanese pond garden, and spectacular annual cherry blossom displays.
Flushing Meadows–Corona Park is a massive public park in Queens, famous for hosting the 1964 World's Fair and preserving the legendary giant steel globe monument known as the Unisphere.

tags.name: Blue Note Jazz Club
tags.description: One of the most famous jazz clubs in the world, hosting both legendary veterans and rising stars in an intimate Greenwich Village room. Dinner-and-show packages are available, but seating is tight, so book ahead for weekend sets.

attractions.description: Radio City Music Hall is an iconic Art Deco entertainment venue located within Rockefeller Center, famous for its massive neon facade and as the home of the Precision Dance Company, the Rockettes.

tags.name: Village Vanguard
tags.description: A tiny basement jazz club open since 1935, where countless classic live jazz albums were recorded. It's cash-only for the cover in some cases and no-frills inside, but the historical weight and sound quality make it a must for jazz fans.

tags.name: 230 Fifth Rooftop Bar
tags.description: One of Manhattan's largest rooftop bars, with a direct view of the Empire State Building and heated igloos in colder months. It gets crowded and pricey, but the skyline view at night is hard to beat for the cost of a drink.

tags.name: Katz's Delicatessen
tags.description: A Lower East Side institution since 1888, famous for its hand-carved pastrami sandwiches and as the filming location of the 'When Harry Met Sally' diner scene. Grab a ticket at the door, tip the counter person who slices your meat, and don't lose your ticket.

tags.name: Joe's Pizza
tags.description: A classic New York slice shop in Greenwich Village, serving simple, thin-crust cheese and pepperoni slices since 1975. It's cash-friendly, no-frills, and considered by many locals the benchmark for a proper NY slice.

tags.name: Peter Luger Steak House
tags.description: A Williamsburg steakhouse open since 1887, known for its dry-aged porterhouse and old-school, no-menu-needed service. Reservations are hard to get and it's cash-preferred, so plan ahead if you want the full experience.

tags.name: Chelsea Market
tags.description: An indoor food hall inside a former Nabisco factory, packed with vendors selling everything from lobster rolls to Thai food to fresh-baked goods. It's a good one-stop option for a group with different cravings, and connects directly to the High Line.

attractions.description: Stone Street is a historic cobblestone alley nestled in the Financial District, completely pedestrianized and famous for its tightly packed open-air restaurant tables and pubs.

tags.name: Fifth Avenue
tags.description: The city's flagship shopping stretch, home to flagship stores for Apple, Tiffany & Co., Saks, and countless luxury brands, plus landmarks like St. Patrick's Cathedral and Rockefeller Center along the way. Even window-shopping here is a New York experience in itself.

attractions.description: DUMBO is a trendy waterfront neighborhood in Brooklyn characterized by industrial brick warehouses, art galleries, and the famous cobblestone photo spot framing the Manhattan Bridge.
Little Italy is a historic Manhattan neighborhood celebrating Italian heritage, famous for its outdoor cafe tables, traditional brick-oven pizzerias, and the lively Feast of San Gennaro.
Harlem is a vibrant epicenter of African-American culture, jazz heritage, soul food, and home to the legendary Apollo Theater stage and celebrated Sunday Gospel choirs.

tags.name: SoHo
tags.description: A neighborhood of cast-iron architecture turned into a dense grid of designer boutiques, art galleries, and trendy cafes. It's one of the best areas to just wander for an afternoon of shopping and people-watching.

attractions.description: Wall Street is the historic financial heartbeat of the world, home to the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and guarded by the famous nearby bronze Charging Bull sculpture.
Manhattan's Chinatown is a historic, densely populated enclave offering visitors an immersive experience filled with vibrant street markets, authentic dim sum, and traditional dumpling parlors.

tags.name: Greenwich Village
tags.description: A historic bohemian neighborhood of tree-lined streets, Washington Square Park, and a dense cluster of jazz clubs, comedy clubs, and cafes. NYU's campus runs through it, giving it a younger, more relaxed energy than Midtown.

tags.name: Storm King Art Center
tags.description: A 500-acre outdoor sculpture park in the Hudson Valley, about an hour north of the city, showcasing massive works by artists like Alexander Calder and Andy Goldsworthy set among rolling fields. It's best visited by car or the seasonal shuttle bus, and plan for several hours of walking.
